data.title: Monitoring
data.tagline: Monitoring continuously observes production metrics, logs, and alerts to find anomalies and judge system health.
data.learningOutcome: You can assign a key user flow an observable signal, threshold, and next step when it becomes abnormal.
data.description: A login error rate can cross a threshold, trigger an alert, and connect its time window, request logs, and running version. This provides signals from real use after release. One test report only records some checks at one time and cannot replace production monitoring.

learning.assumes: You know real users and traffic can reveal conditions not seen in testing.
learning.outcome: You can assign a key user flow an observable signal, threshold, and next step when it becomes abnormal.

distinctions.label: Server logs
distinctions.explanation: Monitoring continuously uses metrics, logs, and alerts to judge system health. A Server Logs is one source of runtime-event evidence that can help explain a failure.

explanation.title: Choose signals that reflect user health
explanation.text: Login error rate, checkout success rate, request latency, and key logs show whether people are affected. Metrics need a time range and threshold, not a dashboard no one can judge.

explanation.title: An alert should return to runtime facts
explanation.text: When an anomaly appears, inspect the version, related requests, and scope, then decide to pause, disable a flag, roll back, or fix forward. Monitoring detects and supports judgment; it does not repair by itself.

data.boundary: Monitoring is neither a one-time test report nor collecting many logs. It continuously produces actionable production signals and alerts; charts without thresholds, version association, or response actions rarely help stop impact quickly.

lessonPractice.title: Ten minutes after a release, login error rate rises from 1% to 18%. Which response best uses monitoring?

options.label: Correlate when the anomaly started, affected requests, and the running version, then decide whether to disable a flag or roll back
options.feedback: Correct. Monitoring links anomalies to actionable runtime facts so impact can stop quickly.

options.label: Check the one-hour average first; if it is still low, keep watching without correlating a version
options.feedback: A longer average can hide a post-release spike and does not show whether the current version started it.

options.label: Roll back immediately at 18% without checking the new version, external login service, or metric definition
options.feedback: Stopping impact matters, but monitoring should still provide basic correlation evidence so the team does not take the wrong action or hide the real source.

data.agentPrompt: Configure production monitoring for login and checkout: define error-rate or success-rate thresholds and alerting, and associate alerts with the running version and related requests. Check these after release; when a threshold is crossed, specify whether to disable a feature flag or roll back.
